headline: A wave of cyberattacks in Japan and South Korea has exposed tens of millions of personal records, and experts say AI appears to be helping the attackers find weak spots.
score_reason: Pool score kept: very large leaks and an official 'emergency' label, but the AI role is the experts' inference and the piece is a broad roundup.
importance_line: Customers of the many Japanese and South Korean firms hit by the leaks face scam and phishing attempts first, then the companies and governments that depend on shared vendors, though the AI link is experts' reading, not a finding in each case.
summary: The Straits Times reports that a wave of ransomware and data-theft attacks has hit Japan, which had over 600 corporate cyber incidents by early October 2026, more than in all of 2025, and South Korea, with the delivery firm Yamato and the media group Nikkei among those disclosing leaks on 16 Oct alone. Harumichi Yuasa, dean of the Graduate School of Governance Studies at Meiji University, says the incidents appear to involve advanced AI scanning for weak spots, and experts told the paper there is no evidence of direct state involvement; this follows our 11 Oct 2026 edition, which carried the Financial Times report that more than 20 major Japanese companies had lost customer data.
notes: Continues the Japanese breach wave carried on 11 Oct 2026 (Financial Times via PCMag); marked NEW because the leaks and statements it reports are from 16 Oct. New today: 16 Oct disclosures, the Arcadia and Scala vendor breaches and the South Korean bank intrusions.
